lesson.title: Us and Them: The Pull of In-Group Bias
lesson.summary: In-group bias is the tendency to favor members of one's own group, whether in judgments, rewards, or even simple perception, and it can operate automatically, without any accompanying hostility toward outsiders.
lesson.body:
Building on the earlier discussion of stereotypes and prejudice, in-group bias is a distinct concept worth separating out carefully. Stereotypes are the beliefs we hold about a group, and prejudice is the negative attitude that can accompany those beliefs. In-group bias is something a little different: it is the tendency to evaluate, trust, and reward the people in our own group more favorably than people outside it, simply because they belong to "us" rather than "them." Importantly, in-group bias does not require disliking the out-group at all. A person can feel neutral, even warm, toward an out-group and still consistently give their own group the benefit of the doubt.

Why does this happen so reliably? One influential explanation comes from social identity theory, developed by Henri Tajfel and colleagues in the 1970s. Tajfel's research used what is now called the minimal group paradigm: he sorted participants into groups based on essentially meaningless criteria, such as a coin flip or a stated preference for one abstract painter over another, groups with no history, no future, and no real stakes. Even under these artificial conditions, participants reliably allocated more rewards to members of their own randomly assigned group than to the other group. The implication is striking: humans seem primed to form "us versus them" distinctions and to favor "us" almost automatically, because group membership becomes part of a person's self concept, and favoring the in-group is one way people maintain a positive sense of who they are.

In-group bias shows up constantly outside the lab. Sports fans rate their own team's fouls as less deserving of penalty than the opposing team's identical fouls. Hiring managers may unconsciously rate a resume more favorably when it signals a shared background, such as the same university or hometown. Political partisans tend to judge the same policy more positively when told their own party proposed it. None of this requires conscious animosity toward the out-group. It can happen through a quiet thumb on the scale that favors "our" side.

In-group bias also sets up the next concept in this unit. If we consistently see our own group as varied, complex, and made up of individuals, while paying much less attention to the internal differences within groups we do not belong to, we end up with a companion bias: seeing out-groups as more alike than they really are. That distortion, out-group homogeneity bias, is where we turn next.
